mcqs.question: For M = [[2,1],[1,2]], the eigenvalues are 1 and 3. What does the eigenvalue 3 tell you about the direction [1,1]?
options: M stretches vectors along [1,1] to 3 times their original length, without changing their direction
M rotates [1,1] to a completely different direction
M shrinks vectors along [1,1] to a third of their length
The eigenvalue only matters for computing the determinant, not for describing the transformation's effect
mcqs.explanation: By definition Mx = λx, so along the eigenvector direction [1,1], M's effect is pure scaling by the eigenvalue 3 — no rotation. Eigenvalue 3 means stretching (not shrinking, which would need |λ|<1), and this is exactly the geometric meaning of an eigenvalue, not just an artifact of the determinant computation.

mcqs.question: Why does PCA rely on the covariance matrix being symmetric, rather than working on an arbitrary matrix?
options: Symmetric matrices are always singular, which makes computation easier
Symmetric matrices are guaranteed to have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, so the decomposition is always well-defined without complex numbers
Symmetry has no special role; PCA would work identically on any square matrix
Symmetric matrices always have exactly one eigenvalue
mcqs.explanation: Symmetric matrices are guaranteed real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, which is exactly what PCA needs to produce a clean, interpretable set of orthogonal principal directions with real variance values. An arbitrary (non-symmetric) matrix could produce complex eigenvalues or non-orthogonal eigenvectors, which wouldn't give a sensible geometric decomposition. Symmetric matrices are not generally singular.
